_why: Machines the simulation stands in for. A screen is the room the window gets (workArea, in the pixels Windows reports at that scale) and the scale Windows applies (scale). On Linux, screen is the size xvfb creates, so there it is a real screen rather than a stand-in. A renderer is a set of Chromium switches choosing how the page reaches the graphics card; artifacts live there, so each can be run on any screen. Nothing here can stand in for a particular card and driver: CI runners have no GPU, which is why misha exists and runs on his own machine.

misha.what: Misha's machine: Windows 11, i5-14600KF, RTX 4060, 1920x1080 at 179 Hz, 100%

fhd.what: The most common screen: 1920x1080 at 100%, taskbar at the bottom

fhd-150.what: 1920x1080 at 150%: less room than a 1366x768 laptop

laptop.what: 1366x768 laptop at 100%, the screen of the 2026-09-04 complaint

laptop-125.what: 1366x768 at 125%: the work area is smaller than the window's old minimum

qhd.what: 2560x1440 at 100%, the screen of the 2026-09-15 artifact report

default.what: What the app does today: Chromium picks

software.what: No GPU at all, the way a broken driver ends up

no-gpu-raster.what: GPU compositing but the CPU draws the tiles

no-compositing.what: The GPU is not used to put layers together

angle-gl.what: OpenGL through the driver: where a lot of driver bugs live

swiftshader.what: Chromium's own software GPU, what CI runners effectively have

pr.what: Every pull request: quick, one screen per system

full.what: Nightly and before every beta or release

misha.what: Misha's own machine, every renderer: the one place a real card is in the loop
